title: Frontend Developer Roadmap
description: A curated, stage-by-stage path from JavaScript and TypeScript to React, state management, data fetching, testing, and full-stack Next.js — ending with interview preparation.
audience: Beginners aiming for frontend roles, and backend developers who need strong React skills.
intro: Follow the stages in order. The milestone at the end of each stage is your readiness check — if you cannot do it yet, revisit the step you found weakest before moving on.

stages.title: Language Foundations
stages.description: React is written in JavaScript, and modern teams use TypeScript. Get fluent in both before touching a UI library, or every framework concept will feel twice as hard.
stages.milestone: You can write idiomatic modern JavaScript (modules, destructuring, async/await) and add types to it with TypeScript without reaching for `any`.

steps.note: Use this as a revision map of the language features you must be comfortable with.
Typed React is the industry default — this course is deliberately React-flavored.

stages.title: React Core
stages.description: Learn the component model: props, state, effects, hooks, and routing. This stage is the heart of the roadmap — everything after it assumes these reflexes.
stages.milestone: You can build a multi-page application with reusable components, local state, side effects, and client-side navigation without following a tutorial.

steps.note: Build every example yourself; passive reading does not build UI instincts.
Routing is what turns a demo component into an actual application.

stages.title: State & Data Fetching
stages.description: Real applications manage server state and complex client state differently. Learn the mainstream tools: Redux for predictable client state, React Query for server state, and Apollo for GraphQL.
stages.milestone: You can choose the right state tool for a problem, cache server data correctly, and explain why a global store is not needed for every piece of state.

steps.note: Focus on modern Redux Toolkit — classic Redux boilerplate is no longer how teams work.
Server-state management is the single highest-value frontend topic for job interviews right now.
Take this if your target companies use GraphQL; otherwise defer it.

stages.title: Testing & Advanced Patterns
stages.description: Senior frontend work is about correctness and reuse. Learn to test components reliably and the patterns that keep large codebases maintainable, plus how the package ecosystem fits in.
stages.milestone: You can write component tests that catch real regressions, and reach for established patterns (compound components, render props, controlled inputs) instead of ad-hoc prop drilling.

steps.note: Write the tests from the course for components you built in earlier stages.
Short but practical — understanding dependencies and lockfiles prevents many debugging nights.

stages.title: Full-Stack React
stages.description: Next.js and Prisma close the gap between frontend and backend: server rendering, API routes, and type-safe database access from a React codebase.
stages.milestone: You can build and deploy a full-stack application with Next.js and a database layer, and explain when server rendering beats a pure SPA.

steps.note: The capstone project of this roadmap — give it more time than the estimate.
Pairs naturally with the Next.js course: type-safe queries from route handlers.

stages.title: Interview Preparation
stages.description: Consolidate with question banks that mirror real frontend interviews: JavaScript fundamentals and React internals.
stages.milestone: You can explain closures, the event loop, and React rendering behavior out loud — not just recognize the terms.

steps.note: JavaScript fundamentals questions appear even in React-specific interviews.
